text:
I want to begin with a broad background rather than with the framework term itself.
Today, AI is moving into more real decision environments, including crisis judgment, organizational governance, public administration, healthcare, and other high-risk settings.
That means AI is no longer only a laboratory system or a stand-alone tool. It is increasingly embedded in consequential decision chains.
So the opening question is not yet what decision architecture means. The opening question is why this broader shift changes the governance problem.

text:
Once AI is embedded in real decision environments, governance can no longer focus only on model performance, safety standards, and compliance.
Those remain necessary, but they are no longer sufficient.
Why? Because failure may also come from the human side: how people interpret AI output, how they change their reliance, and how they act once AI becomes part of the process.
That is why the human-AI interaction itself becomes a governance object.

text:
This leads to the puzzle that motivates the dissertation.
If we care about governance in real settings, we must ask not only what AI does, but what happens to humans once they interact with AI.
People may form different beliefs, they may recalibrate reliance in path-dependent ways, and they may redistribute responsibility even when a human still makes the final decision.
These are the behavioral puzzles that the dissertation tries to explain before I introduce the broader framework on the next pages.
